java-25-concurrency.url: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/ (JLS SE 25 ch.17 https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se25/html/jls-17.html ; virtual threads https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/core/virtual-threads.html ; JEP 505 https://openjdk.org/jeps/505)
java-25-concurrency.version: Java SE 25 / JDK 25 (JLS SE 25; JDK 25 Core Libraries). JEP 505 Structured Concurrency (Fifth Preview) is Release 25, Status: Closed/Delivered, but is a PREVIEW API. JEP 444 virtual threads were final in JDK 21 and are the JDK 25 baseline.
java-25-concurrency.finding: JLS SE 25 sec.17.4.5: 'When a program contains two conflicting accesses that are not ordered by a happens-before relationship, it is said to contain a data race.' and 'If a program is correctly synchronized, then all executions of the program will appear to be sequentially consistent.' JLS SE 25 sec.17.5: 'A thread that can only see a reference to an object after that object has been completely initialized is guaranteed to see the correctly initialized values for that object's final fields' and 'final fields also allow programmers to implement thread-safe immutable objects without synchronization.' Atomicity: java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger (Java SE 25 javadoc) is 'An int value that may be updated atomically'; compareAndSet 'Atomically sets the value to newValue if the current value == expectedValue, with memory effects as specified by VarHandle.compareAndSet'. Virtual threads (JDK 25 Core Libraries): 'A virtual thread cannot be unmounted during blocking operations when it is pinned to its carrier. A virtual thread is pinned when it runs a native method or a foreign function ... Pinning does not make an application incorrect, but it might hinder its scalability.' JFR event 'jdk.VirtualThreadPinned ... is enabled by default with a threshold of 20 ms'. StructuredTaskScope (JEP 505): 'This is a preview API, disabled by default. To use the StructuredTaskScope API you must enable preview APIs' -- compile with 'javac --release 25 --enable-preview' and run with 'java --enable-preview'.
java-25-concurrency.comparison_with_code: Repo compiles at Java 25 (pom.xml:34-36 java.version/maven.compiler.source/target = 25). Safe publication uses java.util.concurrent atomics rather than non-final mutable fields: product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/security/ServiceTokenProvider.java:30 (private final AtomicReference<CachedToken> cache = new AtomicReference<>()) with a ReentrantLock at line 31; same pattern at rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/security/ServiceTokenProvider.java:29 and media-service/src/main/java/com/shop/mediaservice/security/ServiceTokenProvider.java:30. Counter uses AtomicInteger: product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/service/ProductMetrics.java:21 and :26. Virtual threads are OFF by default: utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:9-11 'spring.threads.virtual.enabled: ${VIRTUAL_THREADS_ENABLED:false}'. However monitor-based synchronization exists in main code and would pin a carrier if virtual threads are switched on: order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/OrderReconciliationScheduler.java:203 and :214 (synchronized (this)), order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/OrderCommitCoordinator.java:101 (synchronized (committed)), search-service/src/main/java/com/shop/searchservice/security/ServiceTokenProvider.java:46 (private synchronized String refreshToken()). StructuredTaskScope is not used anywhere in the repo (grep for 'StructuredTaskScope' and '--enable-preview' over all sources and poms returns nothing), which is correct because it is a preview API in JDK 25.
java-25-concurrency.decision: Audit baseline is Java 25. Rule 1: any mutable shared state reachable from more than one thread must be published through java.util.concurrent atomics or an explicit lock, and must never be a plain non-final field; the repo's AtomicReference/AtomicInteger usage already complies. Rule 2: no new structured-concurrency code may depend on StructuredTaskScope because JEP 505 is preview-only in JDK 25 and would require --enable-preview at compile and run time; the repo correctly avoids it. Rule 3: virtual threads stay disabled by default (VIRTUAL_THREADS_ENABLED=false); the three monitor-based critical sections listed above must be converted to j.u.c primitives (or documented as pinning hazards) before VIRTUAL_THREADS_ENABLED can be flipped to true. Rule 4: enable the default-on jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event (20 ms threshold) in the production profile so pinning regressions are observable.
java-25-concurrency.risks: Enabling virtual threads without removing the synchronized blocks would let a pinned carrier thread serialize unrelated requests, producing throughput collapse that is invisible in code review. Using StructuredTaskScope would break the build as soon as the preview flag is not propagated to every module and to the runtime image (Jib). Treating 'no data race' as 'no bug' is the JLS's own caveat: correctly synchronized programs can still be logically wrong.

spring-bean-scopes.version: Spring Framework 7.x reference (the version-agnostic '/reference/' URL currently serving the Spring Framework 7 line that ships with Spring Boot 4.1.1). Bean scope semantics here are stable since Spring Framework 5.0 and unchanged in 7.x.
spring-bean-scopes.finding: Singleton scope: 'Only one shared instance of a singleton bean is managed, and all requests for beans with an ID or IDs that match that bean definition result in that one specific bean instance being returned by the Spring container.' and 'The singleton scope is the default scope in Spring.' Because that single instance is returned to every caller, it is shared across request threads and therefore must be thread-safe (state must be immutable or guarded by java.util.concurrent primitives/locks). Prototype scope: 'a new bean instance every time a request for that specific bean is made... As a rule, you should use the prototype scope for all stateful beans and the singleton scope for stateless beans.' and 'In contrast to the other scopes, Spring does not manage the complete lifecycle of a prototype bean... configured destruction lifecycle callbacks are not called. The client code must clean up prototype-scoped objects and release expensive resources that the prototype beans hold.' Request/session/application/websocket scopes: 'available only if you use a web-aware Spring ApplicationContext implementation... If you use these scopes with regular Spring IoC containers... an IllegalStateException that complains about an unknown bean scope is thrown.' Thread scope: 'A thread scope is available but is not registered by default.'
spring-bean-scopes.comparison_with_code: All 151 @Component/@Service/@Repository classes under */src/main are default singleton scope; there is no @RequestScope/@SessionScope/@ApplicationScope anywhere in the repo (grep over all sources returns nothing), which is correct for stateless microservices and matches 'stateless-session: true' at utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:94. One singleton bean violates the stateless rule: product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/job/ProductMediaSweepJob.java:27 declares 'private int currentPage = 0;' and mutates it at lines 40 and 42 inside the @Scheduled method sweep() (line 29). That is shared mutable state in a singleton, reachable concurrently if the task scheduler ever runs more than one thread or if virtual threads are enabled. Prototype scope is used in exactly five places and only for stateless builders: product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/config/MediaClientConfig.java:33-37, rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/config/RestClientConfig.java:61, media-service/src/main/java/com/shop/mediaservice/config/ProductClientConfig.java:57, search-service/src/main/java/com/shop/searchservice/config/ProductClientConfig.java:38, order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/config/RestClientConfig.java:83 (each @Bean @Scope("prototype") RestClient.Builder). Config values are injected into singletons through non-final @Value fields rather than constructor injection, e.g. product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/service/OutboxRelay.java:35,38,41,44 (batchSize, maxRetries, publishTimeoutMs, claimLeaseMs) and rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/outbox/RatingOutboxRelay.java:31,34,37,40.
spring-bean-scopes.decision: Rule: every Spring bean in this repository is a singleton and therefore must be stateless or thread-safe; request/session/application/websocket scope is banned (these are stateless microservices, not stateful web apps). Rule: @Scope("prototype") is permitted only for stateless, resource-free objects such as RestClient.Builder; a prototype bean that holds a connection, file handle or thread must not be introduced because Spring does not run its destruction callbacks. Rule: the mutable 'currentPage' field in ProductMediaSweepJob must be removed (recompute the page cursor locally per invocation or use an AtomicInteger) before the bean can be certified thread-safe. Rule: configuration must be injected through constructor-bound final fields rather than @Value field injection, so that a singleton's state is final and safely published (JLS 17.5) and cannot change after startup.
spring-bean-scopes.risks: Spring does not manage prototype-bean destruction, so a prototype that owns a native resource leaks silently. @Value field injection leaves a window in which a singleton is published with non-final, not-yet-injected fields; because the container publishes beans safely this is normally benign, but it defeats the JLS 17.5 final-field guarantee and makes the bean's state invisible to the reviewer. A single mutable int in a @Scheduled bean is a latent lost-update: under a multi-threaded scheduler (or virtual-thread scheduler) the sweep can skip or repeat pages.
acceptance_criteria: No singleton bean in */src/main holds a non-final, non-thread-safe mutable instance field; the ProductMediaSweepJob.currentPage field at product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/job/ProductMediaSweepJob.java:27 is removed or replaced by an AtomicInteger/local variable.
No bean is annotated with @RequestScope, @SessionScope, @ApplicationScope or @WebSocketScope; no SimpleThreadScope is registered.
Every @Scope("prototype") bean is stateless and holds no closable/native resource; the five RestClient.Builder beans listed above remain the only prototype beans.

All configuration values are bound to final constructor-injected fields; no @Value field injection remains in singleton beans (@Value at OutboxRelay.java:35,38,41,44 and RatingOutboxRelay.java:31,34,37,40 is migrated).
tests: Concurrency IT that runs ProductMediaSweepJob.sweep() from N threads and asserts the page cursor never skips or repeats a page (mirror of the existing pattern product-service/src/test/java/com/shop/productservice/service/ProductOutboxClaimConcurrencyIT.java).

Static test asserting no @Value injection into non-static fields of @Component/@Service classes.
Context-load test asserting every singleton bean exposes only final fields after startup.

spring-transactions.version: Spring Framework 7.0.x reference (7.0.10 stable on /reference/ at retrieval time). The project resolves Spring Framework 7.0.9 via Spring Boot 4.1.1 (spring-boot-dependencies-4.1.1.pom: <spring-framework.version>7.0.9</spring-framework.version>).
spring-transactions.finding: Proxy-based interception and self-invocation: 'In proxy mode (which is the default), only external method calls coming in through the proxy are intercepted. This means that self-invocation (in effect, a method within the target object calling another method of the target object) does not lead to an actual transaction at runtime even if the invoked method is marked with @Transactional.' and 'For both kinds of proxies, only external method calls coming in through the proxy are intercepted.' Visibility: 'transactional methods in interface-based proxies must always be public and defined in the proxied interface'; 'As of 6.0, protected or package-visible methods can also be made transactional for class-based proxies by default.' Defaults: 'The propagation setting is PROPAGATION_REQUIRED.' 'Any RuntimeException or Error triggers rollback, and any checked Exception does not.' Rollback rules are configured with rollbackFor/noRollbackFor. REQUIRED + inner rollback-only: 'if an inner transaction scope sets the rollback-only marker, the outer transaction has not decided on the rollback itself... A corresponding UnexpectedRollbackException is thrown at that point.' REQUIRES_NEW: 'always uses an independent physical transaction for each affected transaction scope, never participating in an existing transaction for an outer scope... This may lead to exhaustion of the connection pool and potentially to a deadlock if several threads have an active outer transaction and wait to acquire a new connection for their inner transaction, with the pool not being able to hand out any such inner connection anymore. Do not use PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW unless your connection pool is appropriately sized, exceeding the number of concurrent threads by at least 1.' NESTED: 'uses a single physical transaction with multiple savepoints... typically mapped onto JDBC savepoints, so it works only with JDBC resource transactions.' Publishing after commit: '@TransactionalEventListener ... the listener is bound to the commit phase of the transaction by default'; valid phases 'BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK, as well as AFTER_COMPLETION'; 'If no transaction is running, the listener is not invoked at all, since we cannot honor the required semantics. You can, however, override that behavior by setting the fallbackExecution attribute of the annotation to true.'
spring-transactions.comparison_with_code: The repo uses proxy-mode declarative transactions with no self-invocation violations: a scan of every @Transactional method in */src/main for 'this.<method>(...)' calls to another @Transactional method of the same class returns no match, and no @Transactional annotation sits on a private method. Propagation usage: rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/service/RatingEventService.java:40 and media-service/src/main/java/com/shop/mediaservice/outbox/MediaEventService.java:32 use @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED); REQUIRES_NEW is used at payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/service/PaymentWriter.java:26, order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/CompensationFailureService.java:36, order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/impls/IdempotencyServiceImpl.java:105 and via TransactionTemplate at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/impls/OrderServiceImpl.java:120 and order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/impls/IdempotencyServiceImpl.java:45. The connection pool is Hikari with maximum-pool-size default 20 at utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:15, while virtual threads are switchable on (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:9-11) and Kafka consumers run concurrently, so the documented REQUIRES_NEW pool-sizing rule is a live constraint. Rollback-rule deviation: order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/impls/OrderServiceImpl.java:445 declares @Transactional(noRollbackFor = BusinessException.class), and BusinessException extends RuntimeException (utils/common-core/src/main/java/com/shop/common/core/exception/BusinessException.java:6), so this suppresses the documented default rollback for a runtime exception. PROPAGATION_NESTED is not used anywhere (correct, given the JPA/Hibernate provider). After-commit side effects: inventory-service/src/main/java/com/shop/inventoryservice/service/InventoryCacheService.java:25-36 implements the documented pattern manually with TransactionSynchronizationManager.isSynchronizationActive() / registerSynchronization(...afterCommit()) and falls back to an immediate eviction when no transaction is active, which is the documented equivalent of @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true); the repo does not use @TransactionalEventListener anywhere.
spring-transactions.decision: Rule 1: @Transactional is only valid on a method reached through the Spring proxy; self-invocation of a @Transactional method is forbidden and is enforced by a static test. Rule 2: @Transactional is never placed on a private method; interface-based proxies require public methods declared on the proxied interface. Rule 3: the default rollback rule (RuntimeException and Error roll back, checked exceptions do not) is kept; the single noRollbackFor = BusinessException.class at OrderServiceImpl.java:445 must either be removed or carry an inline justification that the method performs no writes before throwing. Rule 4: every REQUIRES_NEW use must be justified against the Hikari pool sizing rule (pool size must exceed concurrent threads by at least 1); with maximum-pool-size 20 the audit caps concurrent REQUIRES_NEW-nested work at 19 and requires the pool to be raised before virtual threads are enabled. Rule 5: PROPAGATION_NESTED is banned. Rule 6: side effects that must only happen after a successful commit (cache eviction, event publication, downstream calls) are registered as after-commit work; the existing TransactionSynchronization pattern in InventoryCacheService is accepted as the canonical implementation, and @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true) is the preferred form where an ApplicationEvent exists. Rule 7: UnexpectedRollbackException must not be swallowed, because it signals that an inner scope marked the shared transaction rollback-only while the outer scope still called commit.
spring-transactions.risks: REQUIRES_NEW inside an outer transaction holds the outer connection while the inner transaction needs a second connection; with a 20-connection pool and more than 19 concurrent outer transactions this deadlocks, and enabling virtual threads removes the natural concurrency ceiling that currently hides the problem. noRollbackFor on a RuntimeException means a failed unit of work commits whatever it had already written, which silently converts a business failure into partial persistence. Swallowing UnexpectedRollbackException makes the caller believe a commit happened when a rollback did.
acceptance_criteria: A static test fails the build if a @Transactional method invokes another @Transactional method of the same class through 'this.' (self-invocation) or if @Transactional appears on a private method.

order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/service/impls/OrderServiceImpl.java:445 no longer declares noRollbackFor = BusinessException.class, or a comment-free justification is recorded in the audit decision record and the method is proven write-free before the exception is thrown.

Every REQUIRES_NEW site (payment-service PaymentWriter.java:26, order-service CompensationFailureService.java:36, order-service IdempotencyServiceImpl.java:45 and :105, order-service OrderServiceImpl.java:120) is accompanied by a documented connection-pool budget: Hikari maximum-pool-size (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:15) is greater than the maximum number of concurrently executing outer transactions by at least 1.
No use of PROPAGATION_NESTED anywhere in */src/main.

Every external side effect that must not happen on rollback is registered through an after-commit hook (TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization with afterCommit, or @TransactionalEventListener with phase = AFTER_COMMIT), e.g. inventory-service/src/main/java/com/shop/inventoryservice/service/InventoryCacheService.java:25-36.

spring-boot-4.url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/ (served 4.1.2 stable; features/external-config.html, features/developing-auto-configuration.html) and the official Spring Boot 4.0 Migration Guide at https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-4.0-Migration-Guide
spring-boot-4.version: Spring Boot 4.1.x reference (the unversioned /reference/ path serves 4.1.2 stable and redirects the /spring-boot/4.1/... path to it). The project pins spring-boot-starter-parent 4.1.1 (pom.xml:9-12), which manages Spring Framework 7.0.9.
spring-boot-4.finding: Configuration property model: 'Spring Boot uses a very particular PropertySource order that is designed to allow sensible overriding of values. Later property sources can override the values defined in earlier ones.' The documented order is: default properties, @PropertySource, config data (application.properties/yaml), random.*, OS environment variables, Java system properties, JNDI, ServletContext init parameters, ... . '@PropertySource annotations on your @Configuration classes ... are not added to the Environment until the application context is being refreshed. This is too late to configure certain properties such as logging.* and spring.main.* which are read before refresh begins.' Binding: 'The properties that map to @ConfigurationProperties classes available in Spring Boot ... are public API but the accessors (getters/setters) of the class itself are not meant to be used directly' and 'We recommend that @ConfigurationProperties only deal with the environment and, in particular, does not inject other beans from the context.' Auto-configuration: 'Auto-configurations must be loaded only by being named in the imports file' (META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports). 'If your configuration needs to be applied in a specific order, you can use the before, beforeName, after and afterName attributes on the @AutoConfiguration annotation or the dedicated @AutoConfigureBefore and @AutoConfigureAfter annotations.' 'As with standard @Configuration classes, the order in which auto-configuration classes are applied only affects the order in which their beans are defined. The order in which those beans are subsequently created is unaffected and is determined by each bean's dependencies and any @DependsOn relationships.' 'we recommend using only @ConditionalOnBean and @ConditionalOnMissingBean annotations on auto-configuration classes (since these are guaranteed to load after any user-defined bean definitions have been added).' Spring Boot 4 migration notes: 'To clarify the scope of spring-boot-starter-aop, it has been renamed to spring-boot-starter-aspectj.' 'Spring Boot now uses Jackson 3 as its preferred JSON library. Jackson 3 uses new group IDs and package names with com.fasterxml.jackson becoming tools.jackson. ... For libraries that require Jackson 2, dependency management for Jackson 2 remains and a Jackson 2 ObjectMapper can be used alongside Boot's auto-configuration for Jackson 3 if needed.' Starter mapping: Spring Web MVC -> spring-boot-starter-webmvc; 'All test starter POMs are named spring-boot-starter-<technology>-test' and 'Given that all test starter POMs bring spring-boot-starter-test transitively, you don't need to define this starter anymore.'

Deviation 4 (Jackson): utils/common-spring/src/main/java/com/shop/common/spring/autoconfigure/Jackson2ObjectMapperAutoConfiguration.java:10-18 registers a Jackson 2 ObjectMapper built with new ObjectMapper().registerModule(new JavaTimeModule()), while Boot 4's managed JSON library is Jackson 3; the offline dependency tree of utils/common-spring shows both com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.21.5 and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind:3.1.5 on the compile classpath. 93 source files still import com.fasterxml.jackson (e.g. rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/service/RatingEventService.java:69 calls objectMapper.writeValueAsString for the outbox payload), while gateway-service is already on Jackson 3 (gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/filter/GatewayErrorResponseWriter.java:8-9).
spring-boot-4.decision: Rule 1: all auto-configuration stays in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports; no class may be discovered by component scanning and no auto-configuration class may enable component scanning. Ordering is expressed only through the documented before/after attributes on @AutoConfiguration, and the audit records that this ordering affects bean-definition order only, not bean creation order. Rule 2: @ConfigurationProperties types only read the Environment, never inject beans, and their accessors are not called from application code. Rule 3 (deviation to fix): replace spring-boot-starter-aop 4.0.0-M2 with the Boot 4 name spring-boot-starter-aspectj at the version managed by Boot 4.1.1, because the repo does use @Aspect (utils/common-logging AuditAspect and LoggerAspect) and therefore genuinely needs the starter. Rule 4 (deviation to fix): migrate the three spring-boot-starter-web usages to spring-boot-starter-webmvc. Rule 5 (deviation to fix): drop the redundant explicit spring-boot-starter-test declarations from the modules that already use a per-technology test starter. Rule 6 (deviation to decide): the Jackson 2/3 split must be closed deliberately -- either move every serialization site to Jackson 3 (tools.jackson) and delete Jackson2ObjectMapperAutoConfiguration, or declare Jackson 2 as an intentional, documented side-car with an explicit ObjectMapper bean; the current half-migrated state (Jackson 2 for payloads, Jackson 3 for MVC) is not acceptable because the two mappers have different default configurations (the hand-built Jackson 2 mapper leaves FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES enabled and registers only JavaTimeModule).
spring-boot-4.risks: Renaming or unpinning the AOP starter changes the transitive dependency set of every module and can break @Aspect weaving if the AspectJ weaver runtime is missing. Moving from spring-boot-starter-web to spring-boot-starter-webmvc changes the managed Jackson starter and therefore the JSON mapper used by MVC, which will change response serialization for 93 Jackson 2 call sites. A half-migrated Jackson setup produces payloads that differ between the REST layer and the outbox/Kafka layer, which breaks consumer contracts invisibly. Keeping spring-boot-starter-test explicitly does no harm but hides which test slice is actually required.

spring-kafka.version: Spring for Apache Kafka 4.1.x reference (stable 4.1.2 served at /reference/; the project resolves spring-kafka 4.1.1 from the Spring Boot 4.1.1 BOM: <spring-kafka.version>4.1.1</spring-kafka.version>). Kafka broker in this repo is apache/kafka:3.9.0 (docker-compose.yml:69).
spring-kafka.finding: DefaultErrorHandler: 'The error handler can recover (skip) a record that keeps failing. By default, after ten failures, the failed record is logged (at the ERROR level).' 'You can configure the handler with a custom recoverer (BiConsumer) and a BackOff that controls the delivery attempts and delays between each. Using a FixedBackOff with FixedBackOff.UNLIMITED_ATTEMPTS causes (effectively) infinite retries.' 'The default recoverer logs the failed record after retries are exhausted. You can use a custom recoverer, or one provided by the framework such as the DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer.' Default back off is 'the default configuration (FixedBackOff(0L, 9))', i.e. 10 delivery attempts. Recoverer failure behaviour: 'If the recoverer fails (throws an exception), the failed record will be included in the seeks.' and 'If the recoverer fails, the BackOff will be reset by default and redeliveries will again go through the back offs before recovery is attempted again.' Fatal exceptions: 'The DefaultErrorHandler considers certain exceptions to be fatal, and retries are skipped for such exceptions; the recoverer is invoked on the first failure.' Boot integration: 'If you are using Spring Boot, you simply need to add the error handler as a @Bean and Boot will add it to the auto-configured factory.' Batch listeners: 'Non-Blocking Retries (the @RetryableTopic annotation) are NOT supported with batch listeners. For Dead Letter Topic functionality with batch listeners, use DefaultErrorHandler with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer.'
spring-kafka.comparison_with_code: The shared listener factory in utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/consumer/BaseKafkaListenerConfig.java:42-48 configures two branches: with a KafkaTemplate it builds a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer (line 43) and 'new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3L))' (line 44, i.e. 3 retries = 4 attempts with a 1 s fixed back off); without a template it builds 'new DefaultErrorHandler(new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3L))' (line 46) which has NO recoverer, so per the documented default the failing record is only logged at ERROR after the retries are exhausted and is then skipped - it never reaches a dead-letter topic, and therefore can never be picked up by the replay service. One service bypasses the shared factory completely: product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/kafka/MediaLifecycleListenerConfig.java:18-28 builds its own ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory and never calls setCommonErrorHandler, so this container also has no recoverer and no dead-letter routing. The services that do use the shared factory with a template are product-service RatingLifecycleListenerConfig.java:16-19, notification-service NotificationListenerConfig.java:17-20 and shipping-service ShippingListenerConfig.java:17-20. The repository's DLT tooling depends on the recoverer being present: utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/replay/DeadLetterReplayService.java:25-27 reads the kafka_dlt-original-topic / kafka_dlt-original-partition / kafka_dlt-original-offset headers that DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer adds, and it is wired at utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/config/KafkaAutoConfiguration.java:54-61. @RetryableTopic is not used anywhere in the repository, and no container is a batch listener (all @KafkaListener methods take a single record), so the documented restriction that @RetryableTopic is unsupported for batch listeners is not violated.
spring-kafka.decision: Rule 1: every listener container factory in the repository must set an explicit CommonErrorHandler with a bounded BackOff and an explicit recoverer. The recoverer must be a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer so that no record is ever lost, because the DLQ replay tooling assumes the dead-letter topic and the kafka_dlt-* headers exist. Rule 2: the no-template branch at BaseKafkaListenerConfig.java:46 must be removed - a factory that cannot publish to a DLT must not silently use the log-only default recoverer; the two-argument constructor (BaseKafkaListenerConfig.java:28-30) is banned in production code. Rule 3: product-service MediaLifecycleListenerConfig must extend BaseKafkaListenerConfig instead of building its own factory, so that it inherits the DLT recoverer. Rule 4: the retry budget is fixed and bounded - FixedBackOff(1000L, 3L) (4 attempts, 1 s apart) - and FixedBackOff.UNLIMITED_ATTEMPTS is banned. Rule 5: a fatal exception (a PoisonRecordException raised by BaseKafkaConsumer.decodeContained at utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/consumer/BaseKafkaConsumer.java:71) must be classified as not-retryable so the record goes straight to the DLT instead of being retried four times. Rule 6: @RetryableTopic is not adopted in this repository; the DLT plus replay endpoint is the chosen mechanism, and it is compatible with the record listeners used here.
spring-kafka.risks: The log-only default recoverer is silent data loss: the record is skipped and its offset committed, so neither the business flow nor the DLQ replay tooling ever sees it. A 1-second fixed back off blocks the consumer thread for the duration of the retries, and four attempts per failing record can push the consumer past max.poll.interval.ms if the batch is large. If the DLT publish itself fails, the documented behaviour is that the record is redelivered and the back off is reset, which can turn a DLT outage into an infinite redelivery loop.
acceptance_criteria: Every ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory bean in */src/main sets a CommonErrorHandler whose recoverer is a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer; the branch at utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/consumer/BaseKafkaListenerConfig.java:46 is deleted.

kafka-guarantees.version: Apache Kafka 3.9 documentation (matching the broker image apache/kafka:3.9.0 at docker-compose.yml:69). The Kafka client on the application side is kafka-clients 4.2.1, managed by Spring Boot 4.1.1 (<kafka.version>4.2.1</kafka.version> in spring-boot-dependencies-4.1.1.pom).
kafka-guarantees.finding: Producer acks (Kafka 3.9 producer configs): 'acks=0 ... No guarantee can be made that the server has received the record in this case, and the retries configuration will not take effect'. 'acks=1 ... should the leader fail immediately after acknowledging the record but before the followers have replicated it then the record will be lost.' 'acks=all This means the leader will wait for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge the record. This guarantees that the record will not be lost as long as at least one in-sync replica remains alive. This is the strongest available guarantee. This is equivalent to the acks=-1 setting. Note that enabling idempotence requires this config value to be all. If conflicting configurations are set and idempotence is not explicitly enabled, idempotence is disabled.' Idempotence: 'When set to true, the producer will ensure that exactly one copy of each message is written in the stream. If false, producer retries due to broker failures, etc., may write duplicates of the retried message in the stream. Note that enabling idempotence requires max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to be less than or equal to 5 (with message ordering preserved for any allowable value), retries to be greater than 0, and acks must be all. Idempotence is enabled by default if no conflicting configurations are set.' Transactions: transactional.id - 'If no TransactionalId is provided, then the producer is limited to idempotent delivery. If a TransactionalId is configured, enable.idempotence is implied. By default the TransactionId is not configured, which means transactions cannot be used. Note that, by default, transactions require a cluster of at least three brokers which is the recommended setting for production'. transaction.timeout.ms - 'The maximum amount of time in milliseconds that a transaction will remain open before the coordinator proactively aborts it. ... If this value is larger than the transaction.max.timeout.ms setting in the broker, the request will fail with a InvalidTxnTimeoutException error. Default: 60000 (1 minute)'. Consumer isolation.level - 'If set to read_committed, consumer.poll() will only return transactional messages which have been committed. If set to read_uncommitted (the default), consumer.poll() will return all messages, even transactional messages which have been aborted.' Scope of exactly-once (Kafka 3.9 Design, Message Delivery Semantics): 'So effectively Kafka supports exactly-once delivery in Kafka Streams, and the transactional producer/consumer can be used generally to provide exactly-once delivery when transferring and processing data between Kafka topics. Exactly-once delivery for other destination systems generally requires cooperation with such systems, but Kafka provides the offset which makes implementing this feasible (see also Kafka Connect). Otherwise, Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default, and allows the user to implement at-most-once delivery by disabling retries on the producer and committing offsets in the consumer prior to processing a batch of messages.'
kafka-guarantees.comparison_with_code: The shared producer configuration in utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/config/KafkaProperties.java:61-73 satisfies the documented idempotence preconditions: acks = 'all' (line 108), enable.idempotence = true (line 111), max.in.flight.requests.per.connection = 1 (line 66, which is <= 5) and retries = 3 (line 109, which is > 0). The service-level configuration repeats acks: all and retries: 3 at product-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:38-40. No transactional.id is configured anywhere, so per the documented rule the producer is limited to idempotent delivery and Kafka transactions cannot be used; the repository instead uses a transactional outbox in PostgreSQL. The retry budget is deliberately reduced from the Kafka default retries=2147483647 (Kafka 3.9 producer config default) to 3, with an outer application-level retry counter (product-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:74 'max-retries: 10'). The consumer properties built at utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/config/KafkaProperties.java:75-82 set group.id and auto.offset.reset only; isolation.level is left at the default read_uncommitted, which is harmless because no transactional producer is used, but it would silently become wrong if transactional.id were ever introduced. The development broker is a single node (docker-compose.yml:69-86) with KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1 (docker-compose.yml:85) and KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1 (docker-compose.yml:84), which contradicts the documented requirement of at least three brokers for transactions. Version gap: the broker is Kafka 3.9.0 while the client is kafka-clients 4.2.1 from the Spring Boot 4.1.1 BOM.
kafka-guarantees.decision: Rule 1: the producer must keep acks=all and enable.idempotence=true, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection must stay <= 5; any change that sets acks to 1 or 0 is a data-loss regression under the documented guarantees. Rule 2: the producer must not set transactional.id, because the deployed topology is a single-node development broker and the production topology is not specified; therefore this system makes NO exactly-once claim about Kafka and the audit states explicitly that Kafka's exactly-once guarantee does not extend to the PostgreSQL write. Rule 3: the exactly-once effect for the database write is obtained instead with the transactional outbox plus idempotent consumers (the outbox row and the business row commit in one PostgreSQL transaction), which is the documented 'cooperation with such systems' route; consumer-side idempotency is therefore mandatory. Rule 4: retries=3 on the producer plus the outbox max-retries counter form a bounded, two-level retry budget and neither level may be made unbounded. Rule 5: if a transactional producer is ever introduced, isolation.level must be set to read_committed on every consumer and the broker must have at least three nodes with transaction.state.log.replication.factor >= 3. Rule 6: the kafka-clients 4.2.1 / broker 3.9.0 gap is recorded as an accepted version risk that must be re-verified when the broker is upgraded.
kafka-guarantees.risks: acks=all still loses a record if every in-sync replica fails at the same time; the durable guarantee only holds 'as long as at least one in-sync replica remains alive'. retries=3 is far below the broker default of 2147483647, so a transient outage will fail the send sooner than the broker would allow and push the failure to the outbox retry path; that is intentional but couples producer and outbox budgets. Leaving isolation.level at read_uncommitted is a latent trap for a future transactional producer. Running transactions on the single-node development broker would fail at transaction coordinator creation, not at the first send, so the failure mode is confusing.
acceptance_criteria: utils/common-kafka/src/main/java/com/shop/common/kafka/config/KafkaProperties.java keeps acks = 'all', enableIdempotence = true, retries > 0 and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection <= 5.

postgres-locking.version: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (16.16 at retrieval time), matching the deployed server image postgres:16-alpine (docker-compose.yml:30).
postgres-locking.finding: Row-level locking (PostgreSQL 16, 13.3.2): 'FOR UPDATE causes the rows retrieved by the SELECT statement to be locked as though for update. This prevents them from being locked, modified or deleted by other transactions until the current transaction ends. That is, other transactions that attempt UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE, SELECT FOR SHARE or SELECT FOR KEY SHARE of these rows will be blocked until the current transaction ends; conversely, SELECT FOR UPDATE will wait for a concurrent transaction that has run any of those commands on the same row, and will then lock and return the updated row (or no row, if the row was deleted).' 'Row-level locks are released at transaction end or during savepoint rollback, just like table-level locks.' Locking clause (PostgreSQL 16, SELECT reference): 'The locking clause has the general form FOR lock_strength [ OF table_name [, ...] ] [ NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED ]'. 'To prevent the operation from waiting for other transactions to commit, use either the NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED option. With NOWAIT, the statement reports an error, rather than waiting, if a selected row cannot be locked immediately. With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work, but can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table.' 'When a locking clause appears at the top level of a SELECT query, the rows that are locked are exactly those that are returned by the query.'
postgres-locking.comparison_with_code: The repository implements the queue-consumer pattern through JPA rather than raw SQL. The outbox claim query is product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/repository/OutboxEventRepository.java:22-26: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) plus @QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "-2"), which is the JPA pessimistic-lock timeout sentinel for skip-locked, over 'SELECT e FROM OutboxEvent e WHERE e.status = :status AND e.id = (SELECT MIN(e2.id) FROM OutboxEvent e2 WHERE e2.status = :status)'. The same pattern is repeated in rating-service .../outbox/OutboxEventRepository.java:22 and :32, media-service .../outbox/OutboxEventRepository.java:25 and :35, shipping-service .../outbox/OutboxEventRepository.java:22 and :32, payment-service .../outbox/OutboxEventRepository.java:22 and :30, order-service .../repository/OutboxEventRepository.java:23 and :33, promotion-service .../repository/OutboxEventRepository.java:23 and :36, inventory-service .../repository/OutboxEventRepository.java:23 and :31. The claim is executed in its own short transaction via TransactionTemplate at product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/service/OutboxRelay.java:67-68, so the row lock is released at commit before the Kafka publish at OutboxRelay.java:95, and the final state update re-acquires the row lock at OutboxRelay.java:137 (findByIdForUpdate) inside another short transaction at OutboxRelay.java:117; a stranded claim is recovered by the lease-based UPDATE at OutboxRelay.java:126 and OutboxEventRepository.java:35-46. Cart locking deliberately uses a bounded wait instead of skipping: order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/repository/CartRepository.java:23-26 and :28-31 use PESSIMISTIC_WRITE with jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout = 3000. notification-service/src/main/java/com/shop/notificationservice/repository/NotificationRepository.java:29-38 uses PESSIMISTIC_WRITE with no lock-timeout hint on a paged retry query.
postgres-locking.decision: Rule 1: SKIP LOCKED (the -2 hint) is used ONLY for the outbox claim and for the outbox final-state update, i.e. only where the documented 'inconsistent view of the data ... used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table' applies. Rule 2: business-row locking (cart, order, stock) must use a bounded wait (the 3000 ms timeout at CartRepository.java:24 and :29) and must never skip, because skipping would silently drop a user-visible mutation. Rule 3: the claim transaction must stay short and must commit before any external call, exactly as OutboxRelay.java:67-77 does, because 'Row-level locks are released at transaction end'. Rule 4: the claim must not be implemented as a single MIN(id) row when several relays can run concurrently, because with SKIP LOCKED the claim then returns nothing while lower-ranked rows are free; the claim must select an ordered candidate set (LIMIT n) so that a busy row does not starve the queue. Rule 5: notification-service findRetryCandidates must declare an explicit lock timeout (or NOWAIT-equivalent) so that a contended retry row cannot block the retry worker indefinitely, and it must skip the contended row instead of failing the whole page. Rule 6: every SKIP LOCKED usage must be paired with the lease/reclaim mechanism already present (claim-lease-ms) so that a crashed worker's row returns to the queue.
postgres-locking.risks: Because the claim query resolves a single MIN(id) row, two relay instances cannot both make progress on the same pending set: the second one skips the locked minimum and returns an empty result, which serialises claim throughput to one row per poll interval and makes the relay effectively single-writer. SKIP LOCKED on the final-state update (OutboxRelay.java:137) means a contended row is silently left in SENDING and only recovered later by the lease expiry, which delays the 'sent' state and can cause a duplicate publish. PESSIMISTIC_WRITE without an explicit timeout (NotificationRepository.java:29) uses the provider default, which is not a documented guarantee. The JPA-level mapping of the -2 sentinel to PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED is provider behaviour and must be proven by a test, not assumed.
acceptance_criteria: The outbox claim query selects an ordered candidate set (ORDER BY id LIMIT n) under SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED instead of resolving a single MIN(id) row, so that two concurrent relays can each claim distinct rows (product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/repository/OutboxEventRepository.java:24-25 must change).

Every @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) usage declares an explicit jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout: -2 for queue-style claims, a positive millisecond bound for business-row locks, and no unbounded default anywhere (notification-service/src/main/java/com/shop/notificationservice/repository/NotificationRepository.java:29 must gain an explicit timeout).
No business-critical row lock uses the -2 skip sentinel; the only -2 usages are the outbox claim and outbox final-state queries.

An integration test asserts the SKIP LOCKED behaviour is the provider's: with one row locked by an open transaction, the claim returns the next free row instead of blocking.

postgres-isolation.version: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (16.16 at retrieval time), matching the deployed server image postgres:16-alpine (docker-compose.yml:30).
postgres-isolation.finding: Default level: 'Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run.' Non-repeatable reads inside one transaction: 'two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.' Update / lost-update rule: 'If the first updater commits, the second updater will ignore the row if the first updater deleted it, otherwise it will attempt to apply its operation to the updated version of the row. The search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches the search condition.' Read Committed limitation: 'it is possible for an updating command to see an inconsistent snapshot ... This behavior makes Read Committed mode unsuitable for commands that involve complex search conditions; however, it is just right for simpler cases.' Unique constraints: 'Adding a unique constraint will automatically create a unique B-tree index on the column or group of columns listed in the constraint.' 'By default, two null values are not considered equal in this comparison. That means even in the presence of a unique constraint it is possible to store duplicate rows that contain a null value in at least one of the constrained columns.' and, under concurrency, 'If MERGE attempts an INSERT and a unique index is present and a duplicate row is concurrently inserted, then a uniqueness violation error is raised'.
postgres-isolation.comparison_with_code: No isolation level is configured anywhere in the repository (grep for transaction-isolation / ISOLATION across */src/main and every application.yml returns nothing), so every transaction runs on the PostgreSQL default READ COMMITTED. The repository applies the documented lost-update rule correctly where it matters: inventory-service/src/main/java/com/shop/inventoryservice/repository/InventoryRepository.java:18-23 reserves stock with a single atomic statement 'UPDATE Inventory i SET i.reservedQuantity = i.reservedQuantity + :qty ... WHERE i.productId = :productId AND (i.availableQuantity - i.reservedQuantity) >= :qty', so the increment is applied by the database to the updated version of the row and the guard is re-evaluated, and :25-29 releases it the same way. Duplicate prevention is enforced by unique indexes rather than by application-level checks: every outbox table has 'event_id varchar(36) NOT NULL UNIQUE' (product-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-initial-schema.yaml:174, media-service .../changelog-002-outbox.yaml:9, rating-service .../changelog-001-ratings.yaml:51, shipping-service .../changelog-002-shipping-outbox.yaml:17, payment-service .../changelog-002-payment-outbox.yaml:17, order-service .../changelog-001-initial-schema.yaml:163), the payment idempotency key has 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uk_payment_idempotency_key ON payments (idempotency_key)' (payment-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-payments.yaml:37) and the notification deduplication key 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uk_notification_event_id ON notifications (event_id)' (notification-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-notifications.yaml:40). Soft-delete designs use partial unique indexes such as 'uk_shipment_order_live ON shipments (order_id) WHERE deleted = false' (shipping-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-shipments.yaml:40) and 'idx_carts_user_active' (order-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-initial-schema.yaml:28).
postgres-isolation.decision: Rule 1: the repository keeps READ COMMITTED, the PostgreSQL default, and does not raise the global isolation level; the audit records that a single transaction may observe two successive SELECTs with different data. Rule 2: every counter or balance mutation is expressed as one atomic UPDATE with the business guard in the WHERE clause, exactly as InventoryRepository.java:18-23 does; a Java-side read-modify-write (load entity, compute, save) is forbidden for stock, quantity, balance, retry counters and version columns. Rule 3: where a multi-step read-modify-write is unavoidable, the row is first locked with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (see the postgres-locking topic) inside the same transaction. Rule 4: duplicate prevention is delegated to the database: every natural key, every idempotency key and every event id has a unique index or unique constraint, and the application never performs a check-then-insert; a uniqueness violation is caught and turned into the documented idempotent outcome. Rule 5: because PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct in unique indexes by default, any partial unique index whose key column is nullable must exclude NULL explicitly (as uk_shipments_tracking_live does at shipping-service .../changelog-001-shipments.yaml:84) and any nullable natural key must be given NULLS NOT DISTINCT or a filtered index. Rule 6: the unique indexes are the last line of defence and are never removed in favour of an application-level check.
postgres-isolation.risks: Read Committed means a multi-statement transaction can act on a stale view of a row it read earlier, which is why Rule 2 exists; any new read-modify-write reintroduces the lost update. Unique constraints that include a nullable column do not prevent duplicates, so a partial index without an explicit IS NOT NULL filter silently permits duplicates. Raising the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE would convert read-modify-write races into serialization failures that the current retry configuration does not handle, so it is rejected rather than adopted blindly.
acceptance_criteria: No service configures a transaction isolation level, and the audit record states that the effective level is the PostgreSQL default READ COMMITTED.

Every mutation of a numeric counter, quantity, balance or retry counter is a single atomic UPDATE statement with the guard in the WHERE clause; a static test flags JPA repositories that read a counter field and write it back.
