redis-atomicity.version: Redis 7 documentation (/docs/latest/), matching the deployed server image redis:7.4-alpine (docker-compose.yml:52).
redis-atomicity.finding: Atomicity: 'Redis guarantees the script's atomic execution. While executing the script, all server activities are blocked during its entire runtime. These semantics mean that all of the script's effects either have yet to happen or had already happened.' and 'Lua lets you run part of your application logic inside Redis. Such scripts can perform conditional updates across multiple keys, possibly combining several different data types atomically.' Determinism: 'the script always must execute the same Redis write commands with the same arguments given the same input data set. Operations performed by the script can't depend on any hidden (non-explicit) information or state that may change as the script execution proceeds or between different executions of the script. Nor can it depend on any external input from I/O devices. Acts such as using the system time, calling Redis commands that return random values (e.g., RANDOMKEY), or using Lua's random number generator, could result in scripts that will not evaluate consistently.' Enforcement: 'Lua does not export commands to access the system time or other external states.' and 'Redis will block the script with an error if a script calls a Redis command able to alter the data set after a Redis random command like RANDOMKEY, SRANDMEMBER, TIME.' Replication: 'In Redis 5.0, effects replication became the default mode. As of Redis 7.0, verbatim replication is no longer supported.' and 'When script effects replication is enabled, the restrictions on non-deterministic functions are removed. You can, for example, use the TIME or SRANDMEMBER commands inside your scripts freely at any place.'
redis-atomicity.comparison_with_code: The repository has exactly one Lua script and it is used for the atomic part of the rate limiter: gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/ratelimit/RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:20-48 defines a token-bucket script that reads the stored token count and the last-refill timestamp, computes the refill, decides the allowance and writes both keys back with SETEX (lines 26-47), executed as a single EVAL via redis.execute(TOKEN_BUCKET, keys, ...) at line 70. The script is deterministic in the documented sense because the current time is passed in as ARGV[3] (Instant.now().getEpochSecond() at line 66) instead of being read from the server inside the script, so the script never calls TIME or a random command. The two keys it touches are gateway:edge-rate-limit:<scope>:<ip>:tokens and gateway:edge-rate-limit:<scope>:<ip>:timestamp (lines 67-69); because they are two distinct keys without a common hash tag, the script would fail with a CROSSSLOT error against Redis Cluster, although the current deployment is a single standalone Redis 7.4 (docker-compose.yml:51-61). No other Lua script exists in the repository: a grep for RedisScript, DefaultRedisScript and EVAL usage across */src/main finds only this class. Bucket4j is not a dependency of this repository (no bucket4j artifact appears in any pom.xml).
redis-atomicity.decision: Rule 1: any read-modify-write on Redis state that must be atomic is implemented as a single Lua script evaluated with EVAL/EVALSHA, never as a sequence of GET then SET round trips. Rule 2: a script must be deterministic - all inputs, including the current time, are passed as KEYS/ARGV; the script must never call TIME, RANDOMKEY, SRANDMEMBER or use an unseeded PRNG, and must not read any state other than the keys it declares. Rule 3: scripts must declare every key they touch in KEYS and must use only KEYS/ARGV for their inputs, which also keeps them compatible with Redis Cluster and with the effects-replication model that is the default since Redis 5.0. Rule 4: because the repository uses a two-key token bucket, the two keys must carry a common hash tag (for example gateway:edge-rate-limit:{scope:ip}:tokens and gateway:edge-rate-limit:{scope:ip}:timestamp) before the deployment can be moved to Redis Cluster; until then the single-node topology is a documented constraint. Rule 5: Redis caches in this repository are plain Spring Data Redis caches and are treated as best-effort, so a cache stampede is handled by the application rather than by a script. Rule 6: bucket4j is not adopted; the Lua token bucket in RedisEdgeRateLimiter is the canonical implementation of the edge limiter.
redis-atomicity.risks: Splitting a token bucket into GET and SET would let concurrent requests each see the same token count and both be admitted, breaking the rate limit under load; the script avoids this but only as long as it stays a single EVAL. The two-key layout breaks under Redis Cluster with CROSSSLOT, which would fail every edge rate-limit call rather than degrade gracefully. A script that read the server clock inside the script would be non-deterministic and would either be rejected by Redis (before a write) or, under effects replication, would produce a refill that depends on replica timing. Redis 7.4 with effects replication means a non-deterministic script no longer errors, so determinism becomes an application responsibility rather than a server-enforced one.
acceptance_criteria: Every Redis read-modify-write sequence in */src/main is a single Lua script invocation; no code performs GET followed by SET on the same key without an intervening script.

Every Lua script passes the current time and every other varying input through ARGV and calls no non-deterministic Redis command; a static test greps the script sources for TIME, RANDOMKEY, SRANDMEMBER and math.random without a seed.
Every script declares all keys it touches in KEYS and reads no key that is not declared.

The two edge-rate-limiter keys share a hash tag so the script is cluster-safe, or the deployment documentation states the single-node Redis constraint explicitly (gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/ratelimit/RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:67-69).

The script source is loaded once and cached by SHA (EVALSHA) or explicitly re-loaded on NOSCRIPT, because 'all scripts may need to be reloaded by the application at any time if missing (after a server restart, fail-over to a replica, etc.)'.
tests: Concurrency IT: fire N concurrent requests against the edge rate limiter and assert that exactly burst-capacity requests are admitted and the rest are rejected (no over-admission).
IT asserting the script is rejected or behaves deterministically when the server clock moves (the timestamp is supplied by the client).
IT asserting the limiter survives a Redis restart (script reload path).
Static test asserting no Lua script in the repository contains 'TIME' or an unseeded random call.

stripe-webhooks.version: Stripe API documentation (current, no version-pinned URL). The repository uses stripe-java 24.24.0 (payment-service/pom.xml:76-79).
stripe-webhooks.finding: Signature verification is mandatory: 'Verifies the webhook request is generated by Stripe using the JSON payload, the Stripe-Signature header, and the whsec_ webhook signing secret from the previous step. If verification fails, you get an error.' Raw body: 'Don't manipulate the raw body request. Stripe requires the raw body of the request to perform signature verification. If you're using a framework, make sure it doesn't manipulate the raw body. Any manipulation to the raw body of the request causes the verification to fail.' Tolerance: 'Our libraries have a default tolerance of 5 minutes between the timestamp and the current time. You can change this tolerance by providing an additional parameter when verifying signatures.' and 'Don't use a tolerance value of 0. Using a tolerance value of 0 disables the recency check entirely.' Replay attacks: 'Stripe includes a timestamp in the Stripe-Signature header. Because this timestamp is part of the signed payload, it's also verified by the signature, so an attacker can't change the timestamp without invalidating the signature. If the signature is valid but the timestamp is too old, you can have your application reject the payload.' Retries: 'Stripe generates the timestamp and signature each time we send an event to your endpoint. If Stripe retries an event ... then we generate a new signature and timestamp for the new delivery attempt.' Duplicates: 'Webhook endpoints might occasionally receive the same event more than once. You can guard against duplicated event receipts by logging the event IDs you've processed, and then not processing already-logged events.' and 'In some cases, two separate Event objects are generated and sent. To identify these duplicates, use the ID of the object in data.object along with the event.type.' Ordering: 'Stripe doesn't guarantee the delivery of events in the order that they're generated ... Don't use created to determine event order or whether you've already processed an event. Track event IDs to identify duplicate deliveries instead.' Response: 'Quickly return a 2xx response. Your endpoint must quickly return a successful status code (2xx) before any complex logic that might cause a timeout.'
stripe-webhooks.comparison_with_code: The Stripe path uses the official SDK verifier: payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/service/WebhookEventService.java:68-69 calls Webhook.constructEvent(new String(rawBody, UTF_8), signatureHeader, webhookSecret) and converts a SignatureVerificationException into BusinessException(ErrorCode.WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID) at lines 70-76, so an unverified payload is rejected instead of being processed; the SDK applies the documented 5-minute default tolerance. The raw body is preserved end to end: the controller binds it as byte[] at payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/PaymentWebhookController.java:33 and passes it unchanged to the service at line 37. The non-Stripe providers use the repository's own verifier, payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/WebhookSignatureVerifier.java, which implements the same Stripe scheme (timestamp + '.' + payload, HMAC-SHA256, constant-time compare at line 64 and line 135) with DEFAULT_TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 (line 21) matching the documented 5-minute window, and it rejects a payload whose timestamp is out of tolerance at lines 50-52. Duplicate delivery is handled as documented: WebhookEventService.handle stores the provider event id (line 88 and line 96) and skips an event already marked PROCESSED at lines 90-94, with a database-level guarantee 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uk_payment_events_provider_event ON payment_events (provider, provider_event_id)' (payment-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-payments.yaml:73) and a DataIntegrityViolationException fallback at lines 99-104. The Stripe event id is used as the provider event id (line 83), which matches the documented instruction to track event IDs rather than the created timestamp.
stripe-webhooks.decision: Rule 1: every webhook request is signature-verified against the raw body before any parsing or business logic; an unverified or unverifiable payload is rejected with a client error and never reaches the service layer. Rule 2: the raw request body must never be re-serialized, filtered or decoded before verification; the controller keeps it as byte[]. Rule 3: the recency tolerance stays at 300 seconds and is never set to 0, because that would disable the recency check; the NTP-synchronised server clock is a deployment requirement. Rule 4: duplicate deliveries are made harmless by recording the provider event id in a uniquely indexed table and short-circuiting on an already-processed event; the event id, not the created timestamp, is the deduplication key. Rule 5: the handler must acknowledge with 2xx before performing complex work. Today the controller performs the full synchronous processing inside the request (PaymentWebhookController.java:37-38) before returning 'accepted'; the audit requires that the Stripe path enqueue the verified event and return 2xx, with the retry scheduler (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/scheduler/WebhookRetryScheduler.java) owning the processing. Rule 6: the endpoint must be served over HTTPS in production and must be reachable without authentication but with signature verification.
stripe-webhooks.risks: Processing the webhook synchronously inside the request means a slow payment update can exceed Stripe's delivery timeout, which makes Stripe retry the event and can cause duplicate application of a non-idempotent side effect. The custom verifier used for the non-Stripe providers duplicates logic that the Stripe SDK already provides; the two implementations can drift apart in tolerance or header parsing. Accepting a stale but correctly signed payload (an intercepted and replayed request) is prevented only by the 300-second tolerance, which depends on the server clock being accurate.
acceptance_criteria: The Stripe webhook endpoint returns 2xx without performing the business processing inline: the verified event is persisted and acknowledged, and processing happens in the retry scheduler.
No webhook payload is parsed, filtered or re-serialized before signature verification; the verified raw bytes are the bytes that are stored.
The verification tolerance is 300 seconds in both the SDK call and the repository verifier (WebhookSignatureVerifier.java:21) and is never 0.
A webhook event id is stored under a unique index (provider, provider_event_id) and an already-processed event returns 2xx without re-applying the business effect.
The webhook endpoint is served over HTTPS in the deployed environment and is covered by an automated test that delivers a modified payload and asserts a 4xx response.
tests: Test asserting a payload with a tampered body, a tampered timestamp or an out-of-tolerance timestamp is rejected (existing pattern: payment-service/src/test/java/com/shop/paymentservice/... webhook tests).
Test asserting the same Stripe event delivered twice is applied once and the second delivery returns 2xx.
Test asserting the endpoint responds within the Stripe delivery budget (for example under 2 seconds) with the business processing moved off the request thread.
Test asserting an unknown Stripe event type is stored as a no-op and acknowledged (WebhookEventService.java:80).

stripe-idempotency.version: Stripe API documentation (current, no version-pinned URL). The repository uses stripe-java 24.24.0 (payment-service/pom.xml:76-79).
stripe-idempotency.finding: Scope and replay behaviour: 'For API v1, Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a given idempotency key after endpoint execution begins. Retries with the same key return the saved response, including 500 errors.' Key lifetime: 'For API v1, you can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned. The idempotency layer compares incoming parameters to those of the original request and errors if they're not the same to prevent accidental misuse.' Key generation: 'A client generates an idempotency key, which is a unique key that the server uses to recognize subsequent retries of the same request. How you create unique keys is up to you, but we suggest using V4 UUIDs, or another random string with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Idempotency keys are up to 255 characters long. Avoid using sensitive data (for example, email addresses or personal identifiers) as idempotency keys.' Valid methods: 'For API v1, all POST requests accept idempotency keys. Don't send idempotency keys in GET and DELETE requests because it has no effect. These requests are idempotent by definition.' Not saved on validation failure: 'For API v1, we save results only after the execution of an endpoint begins. If incoming parameters fail validation, or the request conflicts with another request that's executing concurrently, we don't save the idempotent result because no API endpoint initiates the execution. You can retry these requests.'
stripe-idempotency.comparison_with_code: The Stripe payment-intent creation is idempotent: payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/provider/StripeProvider.java:66 calls PaymentIntent.create(params, stripeOptions(idempotencyKey)) and stripeOptions sets the key with .setIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey) at line 199; the key is also mirrored into the object metadata at line 63 so a replayed intent can be traced. The SDK-level IdempotencyException is caught at lines 68-71 and the call is reported as an indeterminate outcome rather than a failure, which matches the documented behaviour that a replayed key returns the saved response. The key itself is supplied by the caller of the REST API and is validated to be at most 64 characters (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/dto/CreatePaymentRequest.java:16 '@NotBlank @Size(max = 64) String idempotencyKey'), which is inside Stripe's 255-character limit. The same key is persisted locally under a unique index: payment-service/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changelog-001-payments.yaml:37 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uk_payment_idempotency_key ON payments (idempotency_key)' with the lookup at payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/repository/PaymentRepository.java:16 and :18. Every provider implements the same contract with the key (PaymentProvider.java:10, :12, :14), including the non-Stripe providers VNPayProvider.java:38, :57, MoMoProvider.java:38, :55 and MockProvider.java:19, :24.
stripe-idempotency.decision: Rule 1: every outbound POST that creates or mutates money in Stripe carries an Idempotency-Key; the key is generated once per logical operation by the caller and reused verbatim on every retry of that operation. Rule 2: the key must not be reused for a different set of request parameters, because Stripe 'compares incoming parameters to those of the original request and errors if they're not the same'; the repository therefore treats an IdempotencyException as an indeterminate outcome (StripeProvider.java:68-71) and reconciles it rather than retrying with different parameters. Rule 3: the key must not contain sensitive data and must stay under 255 characters; the repository's 64-character limit is stricter and acceptable. Rule 4: the key lifetime is at least 24 hours on Stripe's side, so the local retention of the idempotency record must be at least as long as the retry window of the caller; the repository's own order-side idempotency records are expired by a scheduled cleanup, which must not be shorter than the Stripe key lifetime. Rule 5: idempotency keys are never attached to GET or DELETE calls. Rule 6: the local unique index on payments.idempotency_key is the repository's own second line of defence and must stay in place so that two concurrent submissions of the same key cannot both reach Stripe with different parameters.
stripe-idempotency.risks: Because the key is client supplied and only 64 characters are validated, a caller that reuses one key for two different payments will make Stripe reject the second request; the local unique index converts that into a data-integrity error at a different point in the flow, and the two layers can disagree about which request 'owns' the key. Because Stripe prunes keys after 24 hours, a retry issued later than that window is executed again as a new request and creates a second PaymentIntent; the reconciliation path (indeterminate outcome) is what has to cover that window. A retry that sends different parameters with the same key fails with an idempotency error rather than the original response, which is easy to misread as a provider outage.
acceptance_criteria: Every PaymentIntent.create / refund call in payment-service passes a non-empty idempotency key through RequestOptions.setIdempotencyKey.

The idempotency key is unique per logical payment attempt, contains no personal data, and is at most 64 characters (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/dto/CreatePaymentRequest.java:16).
An IdempotencyException from Stripe is mapped to the indeterminate/reconcile path, never to a plain failure or an automatic retry with modified parameters.
The local idempotency record retention (payment-service and order-service idempotency tables) is at least 24 hours so that it outlives Stripe's key lifetime.
No GET or DELETE call to Stripe carries an idempotency key.
tests: Integration test that calls the create-payment endpoint twice with the same idempotency key and asserts exactly one Payment row and one Stripe PaymentIntent (Stripe test mode or the mock provider).
Test that a reused idempotency key with different parameters is rejected locally by the unique index before any Stripe call is made.
Test that an IdempotencyException is translated into the indeterminate outcome and that the reconciliation job resolves it.
Retention test asserting idempotency records are not purged before 24 hours.

keycloak.version: Keycloak 26.x documentation (server administration guide 26.8.2; securing-apps guide on the 26.8.2/26.7.5/26.6.4 line). The repository runs quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0 (docker-compose.yml:157), i.e. the first 26.x release; the quoted behaviour is stable across the 26.x line.
keycloak.finding: Keys and JWKS: 'The certificate endpoint returns the public keys enabled by the realm, encoded as a JSON Web Key (JWK). Depending on the realm settings, one or more keys can be enabled for verifying tokens.' Rotation: 'We recommend that you regularly rotate keys. Start by creating new keys with a higher priority than the existing active keys. You can instead create new keys with the same priority and making the previous keys passive. Once new keys are available, all new tokens and cookies will be signed with the new keys ... Consider creating new keys every three to six months and deleting old keys one to two months after you create the new keys. If a user was inactive in the period between the new keys being added and the old keys being removed, that user will have to re-authenticate.' Discovery: the well-known configuration endpoint /realms/{realm-name}/.well-known/openid-configuration 'lists endpoints and other configuration options relevant to the OpenID Connect implementation in Keycloak', and the certificate endpoint is /realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/certs. Role claims: realm and client roles are exposed under the realm_access and resource_access keys - 'realm and client roles assigned to the user's organization groups are included under realm_access and resource_access keys, following the same structure as standard Keycloak token role claims'. Direct grant: 'Per current Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security (RFC 9700), this flow MUST NOT be used, preferring alternative methods such as Device Authorization Grant or Authorization code.'
keycloak.comparison_with_code: The services validate JWTs against the issuer and fetch keys through discovery: utils/common-security/src/main/java/com/shop/common/security/config/BaseSecurityConfig.java:79 builds the decoder with NimbusJwtDecoder.withIssuerLocation(properties.issuerUri()), which resolves the well-known configuration document and its jwk_set_uri and refreshes the remote JWK set, so a Keycloak key rotation is picked up without a redeploy; the issuer is additionally enforced by JwtIssuerValidator at line 87 and the token timestamps by JwtTimestampValidator at line 88. The decoder is created lazily and pre-warmed in a daemon thread so that a Keycloak outage at start-up does not prevent the application from booting (utils/common-security/src/main/java/com/shop/common/security/config/LazyJwtDecoder.java:22 and :34-38). Audience validation is conditional: the aud claim validator is only added when shop.security.expected-audiences is non-empty (BaseSecurityConfig.java:89-97), and the shipped default is empty - utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:96 'expected-audiences: ${SHOP_SECURITY_EXPECTED_AUDIENCES:}' - so in the default configuration no audience check is performed; the client check on the azp claim is always active because expected-client-ids has a non-empty default (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:95). Role mapping reads the realm_access claim and produces both the bare role name and a ROLE_-prefixed authority (utils/common-security/src/main/java/com/shop/common/security/jwt/JwtRolesConverter.java:16, :22, :43-45); client roles under resource_access are not mapped. The realm issuer is configured as http://keycloak:8080/realms/ecommerce (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:92 and docker-compose.yml:236).
keycloak.decision: Rule 1: every service validates the issuer with JwtIssuerValidator and resolves keys through the issuer's well-known configuration, so the JWKS endpoint and the issuer can never drift apart. Rule 2: audience validation must be switched on - the audit requires shop.security.expected-audiences to be populated in every deployed profile, because a token minted for another client of the same realm is otherwise accepted (the azp check is a client check, not an audience check, and only covers the clients listed in expected-client-ids). Rule 3: the client-role claim resource_access is either mapped explicitly or the design decision that only realm roles grant authority is recorded, so that a role granted at client level can never be expected to work. Rule 4: Keycloak signing keys must be rotated every three to six months with the old keys removed one to two months later, and the application must tolerate a re-authentication of inactive users; the lazy decoder plus remote JWK refresh satisfies this without a restart. Rule 5: the password grant is only used for the internal service-to-service token exchange (client_credentials) and never for end-user authentication, in line with the RFC 9700 statement that the direct grant MUST NOT be used; end-user flows use the authorization code flow. Rule 6: the Keycloak container version and the realm import are versioned together - the realm file imported at startup (docker/keycloak/import) must be validated against Keycloak 26.x.
keycloak.risks: With expected-audiences empty, a token issued to any client in the ecommerce realm is accepted by every service that trusts that realm, which turns a single compromised or confused client into cross-service impersonation. Mapping only realm_access means a role granted at client scope silently has no effect, which is a frequent source of 'permission denied' reports. A Keycloak outage at start-up is tolerated by the lazy decoder, but the first token validation then blocks on the network, which can turn a Keycloak outage into an authentication latency spike across all services. Key rotation is only safe if the old key is kept long enough for the maximum token lifetime plus the maximum refresh-token lifetime.
acceptance_criteria: shop.security.expected-audiences is non-empty in every deployed profile (docker-compose.yml and the k8s manifests), and the expected values match the aud claim of the tokens each service accepts.
Every service's JwtDecoder is built with withIssuerLocation so that issuer discovery and JWKS rotation are automatic; no service hard-codes a jwk-set-uri.
A test asserts that a token with a wrong aud is rejected with 401 once expected-audiences is configured.
A test asserts that a token signed by an unknown key id is rejected and that a token signed with the rotated key is accepted.
The Keycloak container image tag and the realm import file are updated together and the realm import is verified against the running Keycloak 26.x.
The set of claims that grant authority (realm_access.roles, and whether resource_access is used) is documented and enforced by a test on JwtRolesConverter.
tests: Security IT: a token signed with a rotated key (new kid, old kid removed) is accepted, proving JWKS refresh works.
Security IT: a token with the correct issuer but an unexpected audience is rejected.
Security IT: a token with a valid signature but an expired exp is rejected (JwtTimestampValidator).
Unit test for JwtRolesConverter asserting realm roles produce both the bare and the ROLE_ prefixed authority and that resource_access roles are ignored or mapped according to the documented decision.
Startup test asserting the application context still starts when Keycloak is unreachable (LazyJwtDecoder).

spring-cloud-gateway.version: Spring Cloud Gateway 5.0.x (the project resolves spring-cloud-gateway-server-webflux 5.0.1 from Spring Cloud 2025.1.0, pom.xml:42; the reference /reference/ URL serves the current 5.0.x documentation).
spring-cloud-gateway.finding: RequestRateLimiter filter: 'The RequestRateLimiter GatewayFilter factory uses a RateLimiter implementation to determine if the current request is allowed to proceed. If it is not, a status of HTTP 429 - Too Many Requests (by default) is returned.' 'This filter takes an optional keyResolver parameter and parameters specific to the rate limiter.' 'By default, if the KeyResolver does not find a key, requests are denied. You can adjust this behavior by setting the spring.cloud.gateway.filter.request-rate-limiter.deny-empty-key (true or false) and spring.cloud.gateway.filter.request-rate-limiter.empty-key-status-code properties.' Redis implementation: 'The Redis implementation is based on work done at Stripe. It requires the use of the spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive Spring Boot starter.' 'The algorithm used is the Token Bucket Algorithm.' 'The redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate property defines how many requests per second to allow (without any dropped requests).' 'The redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity property is the maximum number of requests a user is allowed in a single second (without any dropped requests). ... Setting this value to zero blocks all requests.' 'The redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens property is how many tokens a request costs ... and defaults to 1.' 'A steady rate is accomplished by setting the same value in replenishRate and burstCapacity. Temporary bursts can be allowed by setting burstCapacity higher than replenishRate. In this case, the rate limiter needs to be allowed some time between bursts ... as two consecutive bursts results in dropped requests (HTTP 429 - Too Many Requests).' An alternative Bucket4j RateLimiter is also provided by the framework. XForwardedRemoteAddressResolver.maxTrustedIndex(int): 'This configuration exists to prevent a malicious actor from spoofing the value of the X-Forwarded-For header. If you know that your gateway application is only accessible from a trusted load balancer, then you can trust that the load balancer will append a valid client IP address to the X-Forwarded-For header, and should use a value of 1 for the maxTrustedIndex.' 'maxTrustedIndex - correlates to the number of trusted proxies expected in front of Spring Cloud Gateway (index starts at 1).' 'trustAll() ... always extracts the first IP address found in the X-Forwarded-For header (when present) ... This configuration is vulnerable to spoofing via manually setting the X-Forwarded-For header. If the resulting IP address is used for security purposes, use maxTrustedIndex(int) instead.'
spring-cloud-gateway.comparison_with_code: The gateway implements the documented filter contract: gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/config/RoutesConfig.java:38-43 attaches requestRateLimiter(config -> config.setRateLimiter(rateLimiter).setKeyResolver(keyResolver).setDenyEmptyKey(true).setEmptyKeyStatus("429")), i.e. the documented deny-empty-key behaviour with the documented 429 status. The RateLimiter beans are RedisRateLimiter instances constructed with the documented triple (replenishRate, burstCapacity, requestedTokens) at gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/ratelimit/RateLimitConfiguration.java:15-22 (per-route limiter) and :24-30 (global limiter), with the rates supplied from gateway-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:62-72 (replenish-rate 100, burst-capacity 200, requested-tokens 1; global 2000/4000/1). spring-cloud-gateway.decision: Rule 1: the RequestRateLimiter filter is used with an explicit RateLimiter bean and an explicit KeyResolver; the shortcut notation is not used, in line with the documented restriction that the filter 'is not configurable with the shortcut notation'. Rule 2: deny-empty-key stays true with the 429 empty-key status, so a request whose client IP cannot be resolved is rejected rather than being allowed through unmetered. Rule 3: XForwardedRemoteAddressResolver.maxTrustedIndex is the only permitted resolver; trustAll() is banned because it is 'vulnerable to spoofing via manually setting the X-Forwarded-For header'. The trusted hop count must equal the real number of proxies in front of the gateway and must be derived from configuration, not hard-coded. Rule 4: the redis-rate-limiter parameters follow the documented semantics: replenishRate is the sustained rate, burstCapacity is the bucket size and requestedTokens is the cost per request; burstCapacity is always greater than replenishRate for the per-route limiter so that bursts are allowed, and the documentation's warning that two consecutive bursts produce 429 responses is accepted and documented. Rule 5: the Redis-backed limiter requires the reactive Redis starter and is used for the per-route and global limiters, so the token state is shared across gateway replicas. Rule 6: the edge limiter keeps its own Lua implementation because it needs a per-minute budget that does not map onto the framework's per-second parameters; both limiters must return 429 with a consistent error body.
spring-cloud-gateway.risks: A trusted hop count that is larger than the real number of proxies lets a client spoof X-Forwarded-For and thereby evade or poison the rate-limit key. A trusted hop count of zero disables X-Forwarded-For entirely, which behind a load balancer makes every client look like the proxy and collapses all clients into one bucket. Because the Redis bucket is shared, a Redis outage either fails open or fails closed depending on the error handling in RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:77-78, which currently logs the failure and leaves the request unmetered. The framework's RedisRateLimiter requires the reactive Redis starter; mixing blocking and reactive Redis clients against one Redis instance changes the timeout behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Every route that must be rate limited uses the RequestRateLimiter filter with an explicit RateLimiter bean and KeyResolver, and deny-empty-key is true with empty-key-status 429 (gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/config/RoutesConfig.java:38-43).

resilience4j.version: Resilience4j 2.4.0 as pinned by pom.xml:47 and used through the org.springframework.boot:resilience4j-spring-boot4 starter (payment-service/pom.xml:73; resilience4j-spring-boot4 2.4.0 is present in the local Maven cache). The resilience4j.readme.io documentation is the current published line for 2.x.
resilience4j.finding: Circuit breaker exception accounting: 'recordExceptions - empty - A list of exceptions that are recorded as a failure and thus increase the failure rate.' 'If you specify a list of exceptions, all other exceptions count as a success, unless they are explicitly ignored by ignoreExceptions.' 'ignoreExceptions - empty - A list of exceptions that are ignored and neither count as a failure nor success.' 'recordFailurePredicate - throwable -> true - By default all exceptions are recorded as failures.' Retry bounding: 'maxAttempts - 3 - The maximum number of attempts (including the initial call as the first attempt)'; the retry configuration exposes 'the maximum number of attempts', 'the wait duration between successive attempts', 'a custom IntervalBiFunction which calculates the waiting interval after a failure based on attempt number and result or exception', 'a list of exceptions which should trigger a retry attempt' and 'a list of exceptions which should be ignored and not trigger a retry attempt'. Aspect order: 'The Resilience4j Aspects order is the following: Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( Function ) ) ) ) ) so Retry is applied at the end (if needed).' Configuration model: 'You can configure your CircuitBreaker, Retry, RateLimiter, Bulkhead, Thread pool bulkhead and TimeLimiter instances in Spring Boot's application.yml config file', with shared configs under resilience4j.<module>.configs.default and per-instance overrides under resilience4j.<module>.instances.<name>. Observability: 'CircuitBreaker, Retry, RateLimiter, Bulkhead and TimeLimiter Metrics are automatically published on the Metrics endpoint.'
resilience4j.comparison_with_code: Only the circuit breaker is actually used in the repository: @CircuitBreaker(name = "productService") at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/ProductServiceClient.java:28, "inventoryService" at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/InventoryServiceClient.java:39, "paymentService" at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/PaymentServiceClient.java:41 and :62, "taxService" at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/TaxServiceClient.java:34, "promotionService" at order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/PromotionServiceClient.java:49, "orderService" at rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/eligibility/EligibilityClient.java:34 and "productService" at media-service/src/main/java/com/shop/mediaservice/client/MediaReferenceClient.java:31. There is no @Retry, @Bulkhead, @RateLimiter or @TimeLimiter annotation anywhere in */src/main, so the retry and timelimiter blocks in utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:163-173 are dead configuration, and no bulkhead or ratelimiter configuration exists at all. The circuit breaker configuration (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:152-162) sets sliding-window-type COUNT_BASED, sliding-window-size 100, minimum-number-of-calls 20, failure-rate-threshold 50, wait-duration-in-open-state 10s, permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state 5 and automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled true, but it sets neither recordExceptions nor ignoreExceptions, so the documented default applies and every exception that escapes the annotated method counts as a failure - including the BusinessException that TaxServiceClient.java:49 and :52 translate a downstream 4xx into. In the opposite direction, four annotated methods swallow the exception inside the advised method, so the breaker never observes it: order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/client/PaymentServiceClient.java:56 and :80, rating-service/src/main/java/com/shop/ratingservice/eligibility/EligibilityClient.java:49 and media-service/src/main/java/com/shop/mediaservice/client/MediaReferenceClient.java:45.
resilience4j.decision: Rule 1: the circuit breaker may only protect a method that actually lets the failure escape; a @CircuitBreaker method must not catch and swallow the transport exception, because that makes the breaker inert (PaymentServiceClient.java:56 and :80, EligibilityClient.java:49, MediaReferenceClient.java:45). Where a fallback value is required it must be produced by a resilience4j fallbackMethod, which the framework documents as 'executed independently of the current state of the circuit breaker'. Rule 2: the circuit breaker configuration must declare recordExceptions/ignoreExceptions so that business rejections (4xx-derived BusinessException) do not open the circuit; only transport and 5xx failures count. Rule 3: every retry is bounded by an explicit maxAttempts (the shipped value 3, utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:165) and an explicit waitDuration with a capped back-off (wait-duration 1s, exponential backoff x2, exponential-max-wait-duration 10s at lines 166-170); an unbounded retry is banned. Rule 4: a retry is only allowed on an idempotent operation - a read, or a write that carries an idempotency key; the retry configuration is currently unused and must either be removed or applied only under this rule, and the documented aspect order (Retry wrapping CircuitBreaker) means each retry attempt is a separate circuit-breaker call and therefore counts separately towards the failure rate. Rule 5: a bulkhead must bound the concurrency of every downstream dependency so that a slow dependency cannot exhaust the calling service's threads; the semaphore bulkhead is the default implementation and the thread-pool bulkhead is used only for blocking calls that must not run on the request thread. Rule 6: the resilience4j metrics and the circuit-breaker health indicator are exposed through the actuator (the actuator exposure already includes metrics and prometheus at utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:32-43), so an open circuit is visible before it causes an incident.
resilience4j.risks: With the default recordFailurePredicate, a burst of legitimate business rejections from a downstream (for example a 400 because of a malformed request) can open the circuit and turn a small error into a total outage of that dependency for the wait-duration-in-open-state window. With exceptions swallowed inside the advised method the breaker never opens, so a genuinely dead dependency is retried by the caller forever instead of being short-circuited. The retry configuration being present but unused creates a false sense that retries are bounded; if someone later adds @Retry without checking idempotency, a non-idempotent write can be executed several times.
acceptance_criteria: Every @CircuitBreaker method either lets the transport exception escape or declares a fallbackMethod; the four methods that catch RestClientException inside the advised body are refactored (PaymentServiceClient.java:56 and :80, EligibilityClient.java:49, MediaReferenceClient.java:45).

resilience4j.circuitbreaker.configs.default declares recordExceptions or ignoreExceptions so that BusinessException and 4xx-derived exceptions are not counted as failures (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:152-162).

Either the unused resilience4j.retry block is deleted or every @Retry usage is on an idempotent operation with maxAttempts <= 3 and a capped back-off (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:163-170).
A bulkhead (semaphore or thread pool) is configured for every outbound dependency that can be slow, with maxConcurrentCalls derived from the downstream's capacity.

testcontainers.version: Testcontainers 2.0.5 as pinned at pom.xml:72 and used through org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-testcontainers (payment-service/pom.xml:112). The Spring Boot 4.1.x reference documents the Spring Boot integration; the Testcontainers site documents the 2.x line.
testcontainers.finding: Reusable containers (Testcontainers 2.x documentation): 'Reusable Containers is still an experimental feature and the behavior can change. Those containers won't stop after all tests are finished.' 'The Reusable feature keeps the containers running and next executions with the same container configuration will reuse it. To use it, start the container manually by calling start() method, do not call stop() method directly or indirectly via try-with-resources or JUnit integration, and enable it manually through an opt-in mechanism per environment.' 'Note: Reusable containers are not suited for CI usage and as an experimental feature not all Testcontainers features are fully working (e.g., resource cleanup or networking).' Container lifecycle and shared state (Spring Boot reference): 'When using the JUnit extension, container instances are stopped after the test class has run (for static fields) or after each test method (for non-static fields). This can cause issues when used with Spring Boot tests, as Spring's TestContext Framework may cache the ApplicationContext beyond that point and reuse it for another test class or method with the same configuration. If the cached application context contains beans that depend on a container that has already been stopped, later tests or bean destruction callbacks may fail. For this reason, you should prefer managing containers as Spring beans or importing container declarations when the application context should remain usable for as long as it is cached.' Service connections: '@ServiceConnection ... Thanks to @ServiceConnection, the above configuration allows ... beans in the application to communicate with ... running inside the Testcontainers-managed Docker container. This is done by automatically defining a ... ConnectionDetails bean which is then used by the ... auto-configuration, overriding any connection-related configuration properties. You'll need to add the spring-boot-testcontainers module as a test dependency in order to use service connections with Testcontainers.'
testcontainers.comparison_with_code: The repository manages containers as static @Container fields with the JUnit extension, for example inventory-service/src/test/java/com/shop/inventoryservice/support/AbstractIntegrationTest.java:24 and :29, media-service/src/test/java/com/shop/mediaservice/support/AbstractMediaIntegrationTest.java:22 and :28, payment-service/src/test/java/com/shop/paymentservice/support/AbstractIntegrationTest.java:17-18 and order-service/src/test/java/com/shop/orderservice/support/AbstractOrderServiceIT.java:29-30, and it wires the connection manually with @DynamicPropertySource (for example AbstractIntegrationTest.java:40-46 registering spring.datasource.url/username/password and shop.kafka.bootstrap-servers). @ServiceConnection is not used anywhere in the repository (a grep over all test sources returns no match), even though the spring-boot-testcontainers module is a declared test dependency. Reusable containers are not used, which matches the documented 'not suited for CI usage' guidance. Both classes still exist in testcontainers-postgresql 2.0.5 and testcontainers-kafka 2.0.5 but are marked @Deprecated there; the 2.x canonical packages are org.testcontainers.postgresql and org.testcontainers.kafka, and the Spring Boot 4.1 documentation itself uses the 2.x packages (for example org.testcontainers.mongodb.MongoDBContainer). The Kafka image used by the tests is confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0 (for example AbstractIntegrationTest.java:29) whereas the deployed broker is apache/kafka:3.9.0 (docker-compose.yml:69).
testcontainers.decision: Rule 1: reusable containers are not used in CI; the repository keeps the default per-class container lifecycle. Rule 2: because the Spring TestContext Framework caches the ApplicationContext across test classes with the same configuration, every container that a cached context depends on must be declared as a Spring bean (or imported as a container declaration) rather than as a static @Container field, exactly as the Spring Boot reference requires; the shared AbstractIntegrationTest base classes must therefore declare their containers as @Bean methods in a @TestConfiguration, and the @DynamicPropertySource blocks must be replaced by @ServiceConnection so that the connection details are produced by the documented mechanism and cannot drift from the container. Rule 3: the deprecated Testcontainers 1.x package imports must be migrated to the 2.x packages (org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer, org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer, org.testcontainers.elasticsearch.ElasticsearchContainer), because the legacy classes are deprecated in the pinned 2.0.5 artifacts and will be removed. Rule 4: the Kafka image used in the tests must match the broker image used in the deployment (apache/kafka:3.9.0) so that a test proves the behaviour of the deployed system. Rule 5: tests must not share mutable state; static mutable fields shared between test classes are banned, and any test that needs a clean database must obtain it from the per-class container rather than from a shared instance.
testcontainers.risks: A static @Container field whose ApplicationContext is cached by the TestContext Framework can be stopped while another test class still holds beans that depend on it, producing 'bean destruction callbacks may fail' errors that look like flaky tests. Wiring the datasource by hand through @DynamicPropertySource means the property names can drift from the Spring Boot auto-configuration, and a renamed property silently connects the test to the wrong database. The deprecated Testcontainers packages are a maintenance liability: they compile today but the removal in a future 2.x release breaks the whole test suite at once. Testing against confluentinc/cp-kafka 7.6.0 while production runs apache/kafka 3.9.0 hides protocol and configuration differences.
acceptance_criteria: No test source imports org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer, org.testcontainers.containers.KafkaContainer or org.testcontainers.elasticsearch.ElasticsearchContainer; the 2.0.5 canonical packages are used.
Every container that a cached Spring ApplicationContext depends on is declared as a Spring bean in a @TestConfiguration, and no static @Container field is stopped while the context is cached.

The Kafka container image in the integration tests equals the deployed broker image apache/kafka:3.9.0 (docker-compose.yml:69).
No reusable-container configuration (withReuse(true) or TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE) exists in the repository or in CI.

owasp.version: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, current published revision (the IDOR sheet is published as Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html; the earlier IDOR_Cheat_Sheet.html URL now returns HTTP 404).
owasp.finding: REST security: 'Secure REST services must only provide HTTPS endpoints. This protects authentication credentials in transit, for example passwords, API keys or JSON Web Tokens.' 'RESTful web services should be careful to prevent leaking credentials. Passwords, security tokens, and API keys should not appear in the URL, as this can be captured in web server logs.' 'Write audit logs before and after security related events.' 'Consider logging input validation failures.' Webhook security: 'Use the publisher's maintained verification library when available and follow its exact signing format. Supply the raw request body before your framework parses it. Re-serializing JSON, reordering fields, changing whitespace or line endings, or converting the character encoding all invalidate the signature (Stripe).' 'Recompute the HMAC and compare it with a constant-time function such as hmac.compare_digest, crypto.timingSafeEqual, or MessageDigest.isEqual. Never use ==: it leaks timing information and can turn the endpoint into a signing oracle (GitHub, Standard Webhooks).' 'Accept only the signature scheme you expect (Stripe's v1, for example) and ignore any other scheme in the header, to prevent downgrade attacks (Stripe).' 'Return 401 when the signature is missing or does not match, and do not say why.' 'Redact secrets and signature header values from logs and error responses.' 'Require HTTPS on every webhook endpoint and reject plain HTTP.' 'Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher with a certificate from a trusted CA.' IDOR: 'There are three ingredients to an IDOR: An object ...; A reference to that object in the form of an ID, UUID, account number, token or slug; A missing object-level authorization check that allows a user to access or manipulate an object they should not be able to access.' Secrets management: 'Many organizations have them hardcoded within the source code in plaintext, littered throughout configuration files and configuration management tools.' 'Therefore, engineers should not have access to all secrets in the secrets management system, and the Least Privilege principle should be applied.' 'Automated rotation of static secrets: Key rotation is a challenging process when implemented manually, and can lead to mistakes.' Logging: 'The following should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted: ... Session identification values ... Access tokens ... Sensitive personal data and some forms of personally identifiable information ... Authentication passwords'.
owasp.comparison_with_code: Webhook handling largely follows the guidance: the raw body reaches the verifier untouched (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/PaymentWebhookController.java:33 binds byte[] rawBody), the official Stripe library is used for Stripe (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/service/WebhookEventService.java:68), the repository verifier compares in constant time with MessageDigest.isEqual (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/WebhookSignatureVerifier.java:135 and :64), and an invalid signature is answered with 401 without detail (utils/common-core/src/main/java/com/shop/common/core/exception/ErrorCode.java:101 'WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID(..., HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)'). Request and response bodies are excluded from the HTTP log by default (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:72 and :76) and no code logs a token, password or secret value - only the token lifetime is logged (for example product-service/src/main/java/com/shop/productservice/security/ServiceTokenProvider.java:100). Object-level authorization is applied in the data access layer: favourite-service/src/main/java/com/shop/favouriteservice/repository/FavouriteRepository.java:18 'findByIdAndUserId', order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/repository/CartRepository.java:21 'findByIdAndUserIdAndDeletedFalse' and order-service/src/main/java/com/shop/orderservice/repository/OrderRepository.java:15 'findByUserIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc'. Deviations: (1) the custom verifier falls back to a legacy scheme - when the header does not start with 't=' it accepts a bare 64-character hex HMAC-SHA256 over the body (payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/WebhookSignatureVerifier.java:67-75) - which is exactly the 'accept only the signature scheme you expect ... to prevent downgrade attacks' case the cheat sheet calls out; (2) configuration files carry hardcoded secret defaults: the Keycloak service client secret falls back to 'changeme' (product-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:58, rating-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:43, media-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:57) and the database password falls back to 'admin' (for example product-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, rating-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, media-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, tax-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, notification-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, shipping-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8, payment-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8).
owasp.decision: Rule 1: every webhook endpoint accepts only the scheme it expects; the legacy bare-HMAC fallback in WebhookSignatureVerifier.java:67-75 is removed and a header that does not carry the expected scheme is rejected with 401. Rule 2: signature comparison stays constant-time, the raw body is never re-serialized, and the failure response carries no detail. Rule 3: no secret has a usable default value in a shipped configuration file; the 'changeme' and 'admin' fallbacks are removed and the property is made mandatory, as the payment webhook secret already is (payment-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:38 'PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET:?PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET must be set'). Secrets come from the environment or a secret manager, with rotation support. Rule 4: every endpoint that accepts an object reference performs an object-level authorization check, expressed in the repository query (the findByIdAndUserId pattern) rather than in the controller, and each such endpoint has a test that a foreign identifier returns 404/403. Rule 5: credentials are never placed in a URL, a query parameter or a log line; access tokens, passwords and session identifiers are masked or omitted from logs. Rule 6: all traffic, including the webhook endpoint, is served over HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or higher, and the public webhook route in the gateway (gateway-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:45) must be reachable only over TLS. Rule 7: security-relevant events are audit-logged before and after the action, using the existing common-logging audit aspect.
owasp.risks: The bare-HMAC fallback means an attacker who obtains the shared secret can present the older scheme; more importantly it doubles the verification surface and can mask a broken Stripe signature configuration behind a successful legacy verification. The 'changeme' and 'admin' defaults let a misconfigured deployment start successfully with a well-known credential, which is exactly the 'hardcoded in plaintext ... littered throughout configuration files' pattern the cheat sheet warns about. Object-level authorization is only as good as the query that implements it, so any new repository finder that takes a bare id is a potential IDOR. A secret in a URL is captured by web-server logs, which the repository's own logging configuration controls but external ingress logs do not.
acceptance_criteria: payment-service/src/main/java/com/shop/paymentservice/webhook/WebhookSignatureVerifier.java no longer accepts a signature header that is not in the expected t=/v1 form; the fallback branch at lines 67-75 is removed and its tests are updated.

No application.yml in the repository contains a usable default for a secret: 'changeme' and 'admin' are removed and the corresponding properties are mandatory (product-service/src/main/resources/application.yml:8 and :58, rating-service .../application.yml:8 and :43, media-service .../application.yml:8 and :57, tax-service, notification-service, shipping-service, payment-service application.yml:8).

Every repository finder that accepts an object id also scopes by the owning principal (findByIdAndUserId pattern), and a static test fails when a controller passes a bare id to a service without a user scope.

No log statement prints an access token, a password, a client secret or a full authorization header; the HTTP request logger keeps include-body false (utils/common-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:72 and :76).
The deployed ingress and the gateway terminate TLS 1.2 or higher for the public webhook route, and a security test asserts that a plain-HTTP request to the webhook endpoint is rejected.

bucket4j.version: Bucket4j 8.22.0 documentation (released 1 Nov 2026, last updated 2026-11-03). The repository does not depend on Bucket4j at all (no com.bucket4j artifact appears in any pom.xml), so this topic is an evaluation of an alternative, not of current code.
bucket4j.finding: Distributed API: 'ProxyManager is the main extension point that connects Bucket4j to a particular storage technology (a JCache-compliant grid, Redis, a relational database, MongoDB, CouchDB, Apache Cassandra, etc). A ProxyManager is typically built once per RDBMS table, grid cache, or similarly isolated part of the external storage, and buckets are distinguished from each other within it by a primary key.' Usage 'BucketProxy bucket = proxyManager.getProxy("42", configurationSupplier);'. 'BucketProxy is a lightweight handle to a bucket whose actual state is stored outside the current JVM - in a grid, a database, or a key-value store. It extends the regular Bucket interface, so you interact with it exactly as you would with a local bucket (tryConsume, asBlocking(), asVerbose(), ...)'. Atomicity in Redis: 'For all libraries mentioned above, concurrent access to Redis is handled via the Compare&Swap pattern'. 'Bucket4j uses Lua scripts executed atomically via Redis EVAL command to implement the Compare&Swap pattern.' 'Because the entire Lua script is executed atomically by Redis, no other command can run between the compare and swap steps, which guarantees consistency without requiring distributed locks.' 'For the initial bucket creation, a separate SET NX (set-if-not-exists) script is used instead.' Dependency rule: 'The bucket4j_jdk17-redis artifact is an aggregator module and should not be used as an application dependency. Use bucket4j_jdk17-redis-common together with a concrete Redis client module'. Production checklist for distributed systems: 'In a distributed system, requests inevitably cross the boundary of the current JVM ... You should expect this and be ready to receive unchecked exceptions when interacting with a distributed bucket.' 'If you do not want to fail business transactions when the grid responsible for throttling goes down, simply log the exception and continue the business transaction without throttling. If you want your business transaction to fail when the grid responsible for throttling goes down, simply rethrow the exception, or do not catch it at all.' 'Retention tuning is your responsibility ... Maximum cache size ... Expiration policy'. 'High availability (HA) tuning and testing is your responsibility ... you need to test and verify that your system remains available under failure'.
bucket4j.comparison_with_code: The repository does not use Bucket4j. The per-route and global gateway limiters use the framework implementation, Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter, constructed at gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/ratelimit/RateLimitConfiguration.java:15-22 and :24-30 and applied through the RequestRateLimiter filter at gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/config/RoutesConfig.java:38-43. The edge-specific limiter is the repository's own token bucket implemented as a single Lua script: gateway-service/src/main/java/com/shop/gateway/ratelimit/RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:20-48 reads the stored token count and the last-refill timestamp, computes the refill, decides the allowance and writes both keys back with SETEX, and it is executed as one EVAL via redis.execute(TOKEN_BUCKET, keys, ...) at line 70. The script therefore performs the refill-and-consume as a single atomic operation, which is the property the Bucket4j Redis integration achieves with its compare-and-swap Lua script; the difference is that the repository script computes the refill inside the atomic region instead of doing a read-modify-write with a retry loop. The script also sets a TTL (RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:41-45), which satisfies the checklist's expiration requirement, and the keys are per scope and per client IP, which is the multi-tenant key growth the checklist warns about. The current failure behaviour is 'log the exception and continue the business transaction without throttling' (RedisEdgeRateLimiter.java:77-78), which is one of the two behaviours the checklist explicitly allows.
bucket4j.decision: Rule 1: Bucket4j is not adopted in this repository. The framework's RedisRateLimiter covers the per-route and global limits, and the edge limiter keeps the purpose-built Lua script, which already performs the refill-and-consume in a single atomic EVAL and therefore satisfies the same atomicity requirement that Bucket4j obtains through its compare-and-swap script. Rule 2: if Bucket4j is ever introduced, the dependency must be bucket4j_jdk17-redis-common plus one concrete client module (never the aggregator artifact), the bucket must be obtained through a ProxyManager with a stable key, and the CAS retry limits must be configured explicitly. Rule 3: the limiter failure policy must be stated explicitly and consistently - the repository currently fails open (log and continue), which the checklist permits, but the decision must be recorded and the same policy applied to both limiters. Rule 4: key cardinality and expiry must be bounded (per scope and per client IP with a TTL) so that the Redis key space cannot grow without limit. Rule 5: the atomic region must cover the whole refill-and-consume decision; splitting it into a GET and a SET is banned, exactly as the Redis documentation requires (see the redis-atomicity topic).
bucket4j.risks: Failing open means a Redis outage removes the rate limit entirely, which is how the current implementation behaves and is a deliberate choice but must be monitored; failing closed instead would turn a Redis outage into a total outage of the edge API. A per-client-IP key space grows with the number of clients, so the TTL on the bucket keys is what prevents unbounded Redis growth; the script sets it, but the key count itself is unbounded. A Bucket4j adoption would add a new dependency and a second, subtly different limiter semantics to the codebase for no functional gain.
acceptance_criteria: No pom.xml declares a com.bucket4j artifact; if one is ever added it is bucket4j_jdk17-redis-common plus exactly one concrete client module.
Every Redis-backed rate limiter performs the refill-and-consume decision in a single EVAL or a single atomic script; no limiter performs a GET followed by a SET.
The failure policy of each limiter (fail-open or fail-closed) is documented and identical across the per-route, global and edge limiters.
The bucket keys carry a TTL and the key space is bounded by scope and client identifier.
An integration test asserts that N concurrent requests from one client are admitted exactly up to the burst capacity (no over-admission under contention).
tests: Concurrency test: 100 parallel acquire calls on the edge limiter admit exactly burst-capacity requests.
Failure-injection test: with Redis stopped, the limiter either fails open (documented) or fails closed, and the test asserts the chosen behaviour plus the emitted metric.
TTL test: a bucket key that is no longer used expires within the configured TTL and does not accumulate in Redis.
Key-cardinality test: the number of Redis keys stays proportional to the number of active clients, not to the number of requests.
